title: Weyer's De Praestigiis Daemonum: Major Skeptical Challenge to Witch Prosecution
description: Johann Weyer (Wier), a Dutch physician serving the Duke of Cleves, published De Praestigiis Daemonum et Incantationibus ac Venificiis in 1563, the most systematic sixteenth-century argument against witch prosecution. Weyer did not deny the reality of demons but argued that accused women were mentally ill — melancholics whose disordered imaginations made them susceptible to demonic deception without their actually performing real magic. Therefore, he argued, they should be treated medically rather than executed. His work went through six editions by 1583 despite vigorous attack by Jean Bodin, who devoted a chapter of his Démonomanie (1580) to refuting Weyer and accusing him of being a witch himself.
historiographical_note: Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons devotes substantial analysis to Weyer, arguing against the simple reading of him as a proto-rationalist precursor to modern skepticism. Clark shows that Weyer operated firmly within demonological assumptions — accepting demon reality — and that his argument was a medical-theological intervention, not a secular dismissal. The Weyer-Bodin debate exemplifies the intra-demonological disputes Clark analyzes.
source_method: Weyer, De Praestigiis Daemonum (1563); secondary scholarship on Renaissance skepticism and demonology
